title: Getting Around Kyoto: Buses, Subway & Walking
excerpt: Kyoto runs on buses, a small subway, and your own two feet. Here's how first-time visitors can navigate the city and reach the temples easily.
content:
Getting around Kyoto works quite differently from Tokyo, and knowing that going in saves real confusion on day one. There's no single train loop tying everything together — instead the city relies on an extensive bus network, a compact subway, several rail lines, and a good deal of walking. It sounds fiddly at first glance, but with a few basics it's genuinely very manageable within the first half-day, and your IC card ties most of it together.

The lay of the land

Kyoto's sights are spread out: the eastern hills (Higashiyama, Gion, Kiyomizu-dera) on one side, Arashiyama out west, Fushimi Inari to the south, and Kinkaku-ji to the northwest, with Kyoto Station anchoring the south. Because they're scattered rather than along one convenient line, the smartest move is to group sights by area and tackle one zone per day, rather than crisscrossing the city repeatedly. That single habit saves you more time and frustration than any transit tip in this whole guide.

Buses — the workhorse

City buses are the primary way to reach many of Kyoto's temples and shrines, covering plenty of spots the trains don't. They're reliable, frequent, and genuinely comprehensive, with major routes signed and announced in English, including a voice announcement of the next stop that gives you plenty of warning to get ready. The main catch is that they can get crowded and slow during peak tourist times and traffic, so allow buffer time around the most popular sights. Your IC card (Suica, Pasmo, ICOCA) works on the buses — tap on and off — which makes them simple to use without fumbling for coins. On many city buses you board, ride, and tap when you get off.

Subway and trains

Kyoto has a small but useful subway (two lines — one north-south, one east-west) that's fast and beats traffic where it goes. Several private and JR rail lines also connect key spots — for example, the JR line reaches Arashiyama (Saga-Arashiyama) and Fushimi Inari (Inari), and the Keihan and Hankyu lines are handy along the river and to Osaka. For crossing the city quickly when your destination happens to sit on a line, the subway and trains reliably beat the bus, and the same IC card covers all of it without a second thought.

Walking

Central Kyoto — and especially the Higashiyama and Gion areas — is genuinely wonderful on foot, and a large part of the city's charm only reveals itself at walking pace, in the small side streets a bus or train would skip entirely. Plan to walk a lot within each zone; comfortable shoes are essential, as you'll cover ground on slopes and stone paths. The best approach is usually to take a bus or train to an area, then explore it thoroughly on foot before moving on.

Taxis and IC cards

Taxis are clean, safe, and genuinely plentiful — useful for short hops, late nights, reaching a hillside temple after a long day, or when buses are visibly jammed — but they're notably more expensive than in many US cities relative to the distance covered, so most travelers use them sparingly rather than as a default. The one essential thing to sort on arrival is your IC card: load it with cash at any station machine and it handles buses, subway, and trains seamlessly, plus shops and vending machines. It's the key to stress-free Kyoto transit, and getting it set up on arrival — rather than fumbling with it mid-journey on a packed bus — is a small thing that makes every day that follows noticeably smoother, part of the broader route planning that the complete Japan route guide covers.

Do you need a transit pass?

Kyoto offers various day passes for buses and/or subways that can genuinely save money if you're making many separate trips in a single day. Whether one pays off depends on how much you'll move around — for a temple-packed day hopping between several bus rides it often does, while a lighter day may be cheaper on pay-as-you-go with your IC card. Weigh it against your plan for the day, and note that pass options and coverage change, so check current offerings. Either way, group your sights, get an IC card, and Kyoto opens up easily.

Bottom line

Kyoto runs on buses, a compact subway, rail lines to the edges, and your own two feet — all tied together by an IC card. Group your sights by area to minimize transit, take a bus or train to each zone and explore on foot, use taxis sparingly, and consider a day pass on temple-heavy days. Master that rhythm on day one, and the rest of the trip is free for focusing on the temples, gardens, and old streets that actually make Kyoto special.

title: Best Day Trips from Kyoto (Nara, Osaka & Himeji)
excerpt: Friendly deer, a food-lover's city, and Japan's finest castle are all a short train ride from Kyoto. Here are the best day trips for first-timers.
content:
Kyoto sits right in the heart of the Kansai region, with several of Japan's most genuinely rewarding destinations within easy train reach. If you have spare days built into your Kyoto stay, these day trips each add something genuinely distinct — friendly deer and a giant Buddha, a legendary food city, and Japan's finest surviving castle. Here's how to choose between them and what to actually expect on the ground.

Nara — deer and a giant Buddha

Nara is the essential Kyoto day trip, reachable in well under an hour by train. Japan's capital before Kyoto, it's home to Todai-ji, a vast wooden temple housing an enormous bronze Buddha, set within a large park. The park's other famous residents are its free-roaming deer, considered sacred messengers, who will famously bow for the special crackers sold on-site. The combination of monumental history and friendly deer makes Nara a delight for all ages, and it's the one day trip most first-timers shouldn't skip. A half-day covers the highlights comfortably; a full day lets you linger, wander the quieter corners of the park, and browse the shops along the approach to Todai-ji.

Osaka — Japan's kitchen

Osaka is a quick train hop and offers a completely different energy from refined Kyoto — brash, lively, and famous for food. The neon-soaked Dotonbori district is packed with street eats like takoyaki (octopus balls) and okonomiyaki (savory pancakes), and the city adds Osaka Castle, buzzing nightlife, and a warm, down-to-earth character. It's the clear choice for travelers who want big-city fun and a legendary, unpretentious food scene, and it works equally well as a full daytime trip or as an evening food crawl, since it's genuinely that close.

Himeji — Japan's finest castle

Himeji is a bit further but rewards the trip with Himeji Castle, widely considered Japan's most spectacular castle — a brilliant white hilltop fortress nicknamed the "White Heron Castle" for its elegant, soaring form. Crucially, unlike many Japanese castles that are modern concrete reconstructions, Himeji is an original, surviving structure and a UNESCO World Heritage site. It's the pick for history and architecture lovers, and the Shinkansen makes the distance very manageable — the castle is a straight walk from the station.

Other options with more time

  • Kobe — a stylish port city near Osaka, known for its beef, harbor views, and relaxed atmosphere.
  • Uji — a short trip south, famous as Japan's matcha capital and home to the stunning Byodo-in temple (the Phoenix Hall depicted on the back of the ¥10 coin since 1951, and a genuinely striking sight in person).
  • Kinosaki Onsen — a picturesque hot-spring town a couple of hours away, lovely for an overnight rather than a day trip.

Which day trip to pick

If you want the classic, all-ages experience that almost never disappoints, choose Nara. For food and pure city energy, choose Osaka. For Japan's grandest, most authentic castle, choose Himeji. All three connect to Kyoto by train in well under 90 minutes, and depending on your route a regional rail pass (like the Kansai-area passes) can make the fares more economical if you're covering more than one — worth checking the math against individual tickets before you assume it's the cheaper option.

Practical tips

  • Nara is the easiest and closest, so it's the natural first choice if you only have one spare day.
  • Start early to maximize your time on the ground, since even the shortest trips lose real hours to travel both ways and you don't get that time back.
  • If you'd rather not handle the logistics yourself, guided day tours cover all three destinations and can be genuinely worth booking ahead during busy travel seasons.
  • An IC card (Suica, Pasmo, or ICOCA) covers most local trains and buses at your destination, so there's rarely a need to buy separate tickets once you arrive.

Combining two in one day (and why it's usually a mistake)

Stringing Nara and Osaka together, or Nara and Himeji, is technically possible, since all three sit within roughly an hour of Kyoto and of each other. In practice, doing it turns two genuinely enjoyable half-days into one exhausting full day of trains, and each destination ends up feeling rushed rather than savored — Todai-ji's scale and Himeji's grounds both reward slowing down, not racing through. Unless you're genuinely tight on remaining days, picking one destination and giving it real time beats trying to check off two — which day trips make the cut is really a question about how you sequence your whole Kansai stay, the kind of decision the complete Japan route guide is built to help with.

Bottom line

With an early train and a little planning, any of these rounds out a Kyoto stay beautifully — the deer and Buddha of Nara, the food and energy of Osaka, or the magnificent castle at Himeji. Nara is the true can't-miss of the three; the other two depend entirely on your personal appetite for food, history, or both.

title: Best Day Trips from Tokyo (Hakone, Nikko & Kamakura)
excerpt: Tokyo's rail network puts mountains, temples, and a giant Buddha within easy reach. Here are the three best day trips for first-time visitors.
content:
One of the genuine joys of basing yourself in Tokyo is how easily and cheaply you can escape it for a day. The superb rail network puts hot-spring mountains, UNESCO shrines, a giant bronze Buddha, and Mt Fuji views all within a day's reach — no car needed. Here are the best day trips from Tokyo for first-timers, each offering something the city can't, and how to choose between them.

Hakone — hot springs and Mt Fuji views

Hakone is the classic mountain escape, famous for its onsen (hot springs) and, on clear days, postcard views of Mt Fuji. The fun is partly in how you get around: a scenic loop combining a mountain railway, a ropeway gliding over the steaming volcanic valley of Owakudani, and a sightseeing boat across Lake Ashi. Soaking in an onsen with Fuji in the distance is a quintessential Japan moment. It's the best pick if you want nature, relaxation, and that Fuji view in one trip — and it works as a long day or, better, an overnight in a ryokan.

Nikko — UNESCO shrines in the forest

Nikko is a mountain town north of Tokyo, home to a spectacular complex of UNESCO World Heritage shrines and temples set among towering cedar forests. The centerpiece, Toshogu Shrine, is famously ornate — a riot of carving and gold leaf that contrasts sharply with the usual restraint of Japanese architecture. Add waterfalls and lake scenery in the highlands above town, and Nikko is the choice for travelers who love history, dramatic shrines, and forest landscapes. It's a slightly longer trip, so plan a full day.

Kamakura — the Great Buddha by the sea

Kamakura is a relaxed coastal town about an hour from Tokyo, best known for its monumental open-air Great Buddha — a giant bronze statue sitting in the open since its hall washed away centuries ago. Beyond it, the town is dotted with temples and shrines, has a walkable old-town feel, and sits right by the beach. It's the easiest and most laid-back of the three classic day trips, ideal if you want temples plus a sea breeze without venturing far.

Mt Fuji and the Fuji Five Lakes

If seeing Mt Fuji up close is the goal, the Fuji Five Lakes region (around Kawaguchiko, roughly 1h45–2.5h from Shinjuku by direct bus or train) offers the most direct views, with the iconic mountain reflected in the lakes on clear days, plus the famous Chureito Pagoda viewpoint — the classic postcard shot pairing a red pagoda, cherry blossoms or autumn color, and Fuji in one frame. It's a bit further and genuinely best attempted only on a forecast-confirmed clear day, but for Fuji-focused travelers it delivers the picture-perfect shot Hakone can only promise on luck. Hakone is the easier all-rounder; Kawaguchiko is the Fuji specialist.

Which day trip to pick

  • Mountains, hot springs, and Fuji in one: Hakone.
  • Grand historic shrines and forest: Nikko.
  • Easy, scenic, temples-plus-sea: Kamakura.
  • The clearest, closest Mt Fuji views: the Fuji Five Lakes / Kawaguchiko.

All are reachable by train, and depending on your route a Japan Rail Pass or a regional pass can make the fares more economical — though for a single day trip, individual tickets are often cheaper, so do the math.

Practical tips

  • Start early to make the most of the day, since travel each way eats into your time.
  • Check the weather, especially for anything Fuji-related — the mountain hides behind clouds often, so a clear forecast dramatically improves the trip.
  • Consider a regional transport pass for places like Hakone, which bundle the area's railways, ropeway, and boat.
  • Guided tours exist for all of these if you'd rather not navigate the connections yourself, and can be worth booking ahead in peak season.
  • Bring layers — the mountains (Hakone, Nikko, Fuji) are cooler than central Tokyo.

How many day trips is too many

Fitting two or three of these into a single Tokyo stay is tempting, and one or even two is genuinely reasonable — but each day trip costs a full day of your limited Tokyo time, not just the hours spent traveling. Three day trips out of a five-day Tokyo-plus-Kyoto trip means barely two days actually spent in the city itself, which usually isn't the balance most first-timers actually want once they're standing in Shibuya wishing they had more time there. Pick the one or two that genuinely matter to you, and let the rest wait for a return trip — weighing day trips against city time is one piece of the larger route-planning puzzle that the complete Japan route guide works through in full.

Bottom line

Tokyo's day trips add real variety to a trip — hot springs, ornate shrines, a seaside Buddha, and Japan's most famous mountain, all an easy train ride away. Pick based on your interests and the weather, start early, and any of them turns into a memorable break from the big city.

title: How to Ride the Shinkansen (Bullet Train)
excerpt: Riding Japan's bullet train is easy and a trip highlight. Here's how to buy tickets, find your seat, and ride the Shinkansen like a pro.
content:
Riding the Shinkansen — Japan's famous bullet train — is one of the great pleasures of a trip: fast, smooth, punctual, and remarkably comfortable. It's also far easier to use than first-timers expect once you know the basics. Here's a complete first-timer's guide, from buying your ticket to enjoying an ekiben cruising along at close to 200 mph.

Why the Shinkansen is special

The Shinkansen whisks you between cities at high speed, city center to city center, with none of the airport-style hassle of security lines and distant terminals. The classic Tokyo–Kyoto run takes only about two and a quarter hours and is punctual almost to the second — the Tokaido line's average delay has run well under a minute for two decades running, a level of reliability that would be unthinkable for a US train (or, often, a US flight). Beyond being superb transport, the ride itself is a bucket-list experience: gliding past countryside, rice paddies, and, on clear days, a glimpse of Mt Fuji from the window (sit on the right-hand side heading from Tokyo toward Kyoto/Osaka for the best chance).

Buying tickets

  • With a Japan Rail Pass: the pass covers most Shinkansen (with exceptions for the very fastest Nozomi/Mizuho services, which need a supplement) — reserve seats for free at JR ticket offices or machines, or simply ride the non-reserved cars.
  • Without a pass: buy a ticket at JR ticket machines (English menus available) or ticket offices for your route. You'll typically get a base fare ticket plus a limited-express (Shinkansen) ticket — feed both through the gate together.
  • Reserved vs non-reserved: a reserved seat (shitei-seki) guarantees you a spot and is worth it in busy periods and holidays; non-reserved cars (jiyu-seki) are first-come and cheaper, fine off-peak. You can also book some routes online in advance.

At the station

  • Look for the dedicated Shinkansen gates and platforms — they're separate from regular train gates and clearly signed in English.
  • Insert your ticket(s) into the gate together (with a pass, use the staffed gate or tap as directed).
  • Platform displays show your train, its exact departure time, and where each car stops — line up at your car number marked on the platform floor.
  • Trains stop only briefly, so be ready to board promptly at your marked spot.

Finding and using your seat

  • Cars are numbered; a reserved ticket shows your car and seat number.
  • Non-reserved seating is in specific cars (shown on signage, often cars 1–3) — board those and take any free seat.
  • There's generous legroom, fold-down trays, power outlets at most seats, and overhead racks for smaller bags.
  • Seats can often be rotated to face your group — there's a foot pedal or lever, or staff will help.

Luggage: the oversized-baggage rule

One rule worth knowing in advance: on the Tokaido, Sanyo, and Kyushu Shinkansen lines (the main routes including Tokyo–Kyoto–Osaka–Hiroshima–Fukuoka), large luggage with total dimensions over 160 cm (length + width + height) requires a free reservation for an "oversized baggage" seat — a regular reserved seat with dedicated space behind it. Reserving it costs nothing, but boarding with such a bag without the reservation can incur a fee. Most normal suitcases are fine in the overhead racks or the space behind the last row; this rule targets the biggest bags. If you're traveling with large luggage, just request the oversized-baggage seat when you reserve.

Onboard etiquette and tips

  • Keep quiet — conversations are low, phones on silent, and calls taken standing in the vestibules between cars, not at your seat.
  • It's customary and delightful to enjoy an ekiben (a station bento box) on board — buy one at the station beforehand along with a drink; it's part of the experience.
  • Recline considerately (a glance back is polite) and keep aisles clear.
  • Trains depart exactly on time — be on the platform a few minutes early.
  • There are restrooms, and on some trains a trolley service or vending.

Practical notes

  • Arrive with a few minutes to spare to find your car's queue spot on the platform.
  • The fastest Nozomi and Mizuho services aren't covered by the standard nationwide JR Pass without paying a supplement — the slightly slower Hikari and Sakura are covered and only a few minutes longer on most routes.
  • Keep all ticket pieces until you've exited the gate at your destination.
  • Reserve the oversized-baggage spot in advance if you're carrying a large suitcase.

Bottom line

The Shinkansen is fast, effortless, and a genuine joy to ride. Buy your ticket (or use your pass), find the Shinkansen platform, line up at your car number, grab an ekiben, mind the luggage rule if your bag is large, and settle in for one of the smoothest, most iconic train journeys in the world — and once you've ridden it once, deciding how many more times to ride it (versus flying or bussing between cities) becomes part of the bigger route-planning picture that the complete Japan route guide works through in detail.

title: Renting a Car in Japan: What to Know
excerpt: Most first-timers don't need a car in Japan, but for rural trips it helps. Here's what to know — the IDP requirement, driving on the left, and more.
content:
For most first-time visitors doing a Tokyo–Kyoto trip, you don't need a car — Japan's trains are faster, cheaper, and far less stressful, and city driving is more hassle than help. But for rural regions, certain countryside itineraries, or maximum flexibility off the rail network, renting a car can genuinely make sense. Here's what to know before you do.

Do you actually need one?

Japan is extremely rail-centric, and the train network reaches the overwhelming majority of places travelers want to go quickly and conveniently. In cities, driving is not recommended — traffic, expensive and scarce parking, narrow streets, and excellent public transit make a car a burden rather than a help. Consider renting only if you're exploring genuinely rural areas: much of rural Hokkaido, the Japanese Alps (the Kamikochi valley itself is closed to private cars, but the surrounding region rewards a rental), the Noto Peninsula, remote Kyushu coastlines, and any region where attractions sit miles apart and buses run only a handful of times a day. For the classic city-based first trip, the trains win every time — save the car for a second or third trip built specifically around the countryside.

The essential requirement: an International Driving Permit

To legally drive in Japan as a visitor, you need an International Driving Permit (IDP) to accompany your valid home driver's license — both must be carried while driving. There's a detail worth knowing precisely: Japan recognizes only IDPs issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention, not the newer 1968 Vienna Convention that many other countries' permits are based on. This is exactly what trips up travelers from several European countries, whose home IDPs simply aren't valid in Japan. Americans are covered by default, since the AAA-issued US IDP is the 1949 version. Crucially, you must obtain the IDP in your home country before you leave — through AAA in the US — since it cannot be obtained once you're in Japan, and driving without one is treated as a real offense, not a formality: fines up to roughly ¥300,000 (around $2,000), potential vehicle impoundment, and enforcement that's genuinely active, with police checking permits at routine stops. An IDP is valid for one year from its issue date, so if you're planning a trip more than a year out, get it closer to departure rather than far in advance.

Driving on the left

Japan drives on the left, with the steering wheel on the right — which takes real adjustment if you're used to driving on the right side. Take it slow at first, especially at intersections, when turning (it's easy to instinctively drift to the wrong side), and with the wipers-vs-indicators muscle memory, since the stalks are typically mirrored from a US car. Roads are generally well maintained, orderly, and signed, with many signs in English on expressways and major routes, and Japanese drivers are typically calm, patient, and courteous — noticeably less aggressive than typical US city driving, which helps ease the adjustment.

Other key rules and notes

  • Zero-tolerance drink-driving: Japan has extremely strict drink-driving laws — effectively, do not consume any alcohol before driving. Penalties are severe, and they can extend to passengers who knowingly let an impaired person drive, and even to anyone who supplied the alcohol.
  • Tolls: expressways are tolled and can add up meaningfully over a long countryside route; rentals usually offer an ETC card for automatic electronic toll payment (no stopping to pay cash), which is worth taking for any multi-day trip.
  • Navigation: rental cars have GPS, often with an English-language mode, and you can frequently set a destination by phone number or Japan's "map code" system rather than typing an address.
  • Parking: often paid, limited, and sometimes booked via coin lots or multi-level tower parking, especially in towns; factor it into your plans and budget, since it's rarely free the way it might be at a US rural attraction.
  • Fuel: gas stations are widely available on main routes; know whether yours is full-service or self-service (both exist), and note stations can be sparser in genuinely remote areas, so don't let the tank run too low.
  • Snow: in winter, mountain and northern regions need winter tires or chains — confirm this is arranged with the rental company before you go, since summer tires on a snowy mountain road are genuinely dangerous.

Renting practically

  • Book in advance, especially in peak seasons (cherry blossom, Golden Week, Obon, autumn foliage) and for larger vehicles or automatics, which can sell out at smaller rural counters.
  • Bring your home license, the IDP, and your passport to pick up the car — all three are required, and missing any one of them means no car.
  • Inspect the car for existing damage and understand the insurance/CDW options before driving off; basic coverage is often included, but a higher tier reduces your liability substantially for not much extra cost.
  • Allow time to get comfortable with left-side driving in a quiet lot or side street before tackling busier roads or an expressway on-ramp.
  • Consider a one-way rental if you're picking up in one city and dropping off in another — most major companies support it, typically for an extra fee that scales with the distance between locations.

Bottom line

Skip the car for a classic city-based first trip — the trains are simply better, and nothing about renting a car changes that math. But for rural exploration where rail doesn't reach, a rental unlocks places you otherwise couldn't easily see. If you go that route, get your 1949-Convention International Driving Permit before leaving home, remember to drive on the left, never drink and drive, and budget for tolls and parking. Used in the right places, a car can be a wonderful way to discover Japan's countryside at your own pace.
